ours.title: Lynching of Oscar Coger
ours.accusation: accused of incendiarism
ours.lead: The lynching of Oscar Coger was the hanging of a Black man by neighbors at Cherokee, Colbert County, Alabama, in late December 1887. Coger, accused of trying twice to set fire to the house of a widow, Mrs. Lindsay, was caught by men watching the house and hanged from a tree limb. A Montgomery Advertiser dispatch carried the story across the country, and a later local report said that men arrested for the lynching were released when no prosecutor appeared.

ours.title: Lynching of old man Kelly
ours.lead: The lynching of old man Kelly was the reported hanging of the elder member of the Kelly family of "No Man's Land" by pursuing vigilantes in the Texas Panhandle, described in dispatches dated January 2 to 4, 1888. According to these reports, the vigilantes overtook him after a long chase, hanged him, let him down until he confessed that his family had killed and robbed nine men and two women, and hanged him again. Papers from West Virginia to Montana ran it as the end of the Kelly murder case, but the Wichita Eagle called the Kelly stories "fabrications."

ours.title: Madisonville lynchings (1888)
ours.accusation: said to have been lawless: threats against citizens, theft, arson, murder of witnesses (Page called a notorious sneak thief)
ours.lead: The Madisonville lynchings were the killing of William "Bill" Bobo and the hanging of Reden S. "Red" Page by a body of several hundred armed citizens at Madisonville, the seat of Madison County, Texas, on January 3, 1888. They also fired on Alf Whitten and warned others to leave, and Governor Ross sent the Navasota Guards. Texas correspondents defended the killings as a rising against a gang of horse and cattle thieves, while a national wire report described "Reformers" killing men who favored saloons.

ours.title: Caldwell jail lynching (1888)
ours.accusation: said to have murdered planter Alvord
ours.lead: The Caldwell jail lynching was the shooting of Mexican prisoners in the jail at Caldwell, Texas, by a mob on the night of January 14 or 15, 1888. The prisoners were held on a charge of murdering a local planter, and at least one of them was killed. The Fort Worth Gazette reported one man dead and another dangerously wounded, while a Galveston wire and later news briefs spread the story nationally as the lynching of "two Mexican murderers."

ours.title: Abduction of Henry Burney
ours.accusation: accused of robbery
ours.lead: The abduction of Henry Burney was the removal of a Black prisoner from the Laurens County jail at Dublin, Georgia, by a party of masked men on the night of Tuesday, January 10, 1888. Burney was being held on a charge of knocking down and robbing J. M. Reinhart of Dublin. Georgia papers said only that he was believed, or possibly, lynched, while national news summaries reported flatly that he had been lynched, placing the event in Laurens County, Kentucky, or at Macon. A month later a Savannah paper reported that he had been sentenced to four years' imprisonment.

ours.title: Lynching of "Nosey" Smith
ours.accusation: said to have shamefully abused his two daughters
ours.lead: The lynching of "Nosey" Smith was the hanging of a man by vigilantes at Sun River, Montana Territory, reported in January 1888. According to a dispatch from Macleod in the Northwest Territories, he was accused of having shamefully abused his two daughters and was hanged after returning to Montana to get them back. The brief item ran in papers from Virginia to Oregon, and a year-end tally later counted him among the year's victims of "Judge Lynch."

ours.title: Limestone bank robbery lynching
victims: unnamed leader of the bank robbers
ours.accusation: accused of bank robbery and murder of the cashier W T Reynolds
ours.lead: The Limestone bank robbery lynching was the reported hanging of an unnamed robber by a "Judge Lynch" court at Limestone, Indian Territory, in January 1888, after four masked men robbed the Citizens' Bank and killed its cashier, W. T. Reynolds. According to a widely reprinted despatch, a second robber, Thomas Evan, was shot dead in a gunfight with townspeople, and the two remaining robbers were sent to Fort Washita for the federal authorities. The story ran in papers from South Carolina to Wyoming, but a letter from Atoka printed in the Fort Worth Gazette said there had never been a bank, or a town, at Limestone Gap.

ours.title: Lynching of Santos Salizer
ours.accusation: said to have murdered Jacob Stafford
ours.lead: The lynching of Santos Salizer was the reported hanging of a Mexican man near Collins, in Nueces County, Texas, on the night of Sunday, January 22, 1888. He was accused of murdering Jacob Stafford, a sheep raiser whose body had been found in a water hole the day before. The story reached Corpus Christi only as a report, yet it ran in papers across the country, several of which headlined the slight evidence on which he was said to have been killed.

ours.title: Plymouth triple lynching
ours.accusation: accused of murdering the jeweler E. Dawman
ours.lead: The Plymouth triple lynching was the killing of three Black prisoners, Matthew Blount, his brother Jack Blount and Patterson Spruill, by masked men at Plymouth, Washington County, North Carolina, around midnight on Thursday, January 26, 1888. Held on a charge of murdering a traveling peddler near Creswell, the men were taken from the jailer, tied to trees about a mile from town and shot to death. The killing was reported nationally by wire, a Raleigh correspondent called it the state's first lynching in many months, and no lyncher was identified.

Dunce was held for the killing of W. R. Wilson at Russellville, Alabama, a few weeks earlier. The news travelled as a one-sentence telegraph item that ran in papers across the country within a week.

ours.title: Lynching of Ben Edwards
ours.accusation: said to have grossly assaulted Miss Catharine Hughes, a white girl, on Friday last
ours.lead: The lynching of Ben Edwards took place at Amite City, Louisiana, on the night of January 28, 1888, when a body of about 100 armed men took Edwards, a Black man, from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. Edwards had been jailed on the accusation that he had criminally assaulted Catherine Hughes, a white girl who lived near the town. A dispatch from Amite City to the New Orleans Times-Democrat ran in papers from California to South Carolina, often under headlines such as "A Fiend Quickly Disposed Of."

ours.title: Lynching at Ponchatoula, 1888
ours.accusation: accused of assault on a young girl
ours.lead: The lynching at Ponchatoula was the hanging of an unnamed Black man near Ponchatoula, Tangipahoa Parish, Louisiana, on the night of February 8, 1888. Accused of breaking into a white man's house and assaulting his young daughter, he was taken from officers who were bringing him to the parish jail and was hanged to a tree. A New Orleans dispatch counted it as the second lynching in Tangipahoa Parish within ten days, and the placard left on the body, "We Protect Our Women," served as the headline over the story in at least two papers.

ours.title: Lynching of Alonzo Holly
ours.accusation: accused of criminally assaulting a white woman
ours.lead: The lynching of Alonzo Holly took place at Pinckneyville, Perry County, Illinois, early on February 14, 1888, when masked men took Holly, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from a tree nearby. Holly was held on a charge of assaulting a white woman near St. Johns. A Pinckneyville correspondent called it "the first lynching that ever occurred in Perry county," and wire dispatches carried it nationwide within a day.

ours.title: Killing of Hunley Royl
ours.lead: The killing of Hunley Royl was the assassination of an elderly Black man living near Newport, Arkansas, by a party of masked men, reported in early March 1888. The only account found is a single line in a weekly state news column, which gave no date, motive or follow-up.

ours.title: Spanish Camp massacre
ours.lead: The Spanish Camp massacre was the killing of Black residents at Spanish Camp, Wharton County, Texas, early on Sunday, February 26, 1888, when attackers fired a cabin and shot its occupants as they fled. Later reports put the dead at seven of the eight people inside, and the body of a Black man, William Battle, was found hanging nearby. The killings, traced to a land suit the Black residents had won, drew national wire coverage, a Texas editorial dispute over the governor's response, arrests, and mention in the United States Senate.

Wire reports carried the double lynching nationally, and a later dispatch drew notice by reporting that Price revived after being cut down and was hanged again.

ours.title: Lynching of Tom Forsythe
ours.accusation: accused of the murder of County Treasurer Hill (had confessed)
ours.lead: The lynching of Tom Forsythe took place at Carthage, Panola County, Texas, on the night of February 28-29, 1888, when about 400 men took the sheriff's son from jail and hanged him. Forsythe had been arrested days earlier and was reported to have confessed to the murder and robbery of County Treasurer D. C. Hill. The case drew notice because the lynchers acted unmasked and laid the body in the victim's blood, and because Governor Ross rebuked them.

ours.title: Lynching of Charles Duncan
ours.accusation: said to have shot Milt Hawks
ours.lead: The lynching of Charles Duncan took place in McDowell County, West Virginia, in early March 1888, when a mob took Duncan from officers who were carrying him to jail and hanged him to a tree. Duncan had been accused of shooting Milt Hawks, the man he lived with, during a quarrel between Hawks and his wife. A Parkersburg dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and the Evening Star of Washington predicted that nothing would be done about it.

ours.title: Killing of Margaret Auxier
ours.lead: The killing of Margaret Auxier was the shooting death of a young woman by a party of men at her father's house near Yocum, Morgan County, Kentucky, in early March 1888. Several men were held on suspicion and lynching was talked of, and in August a man charged with the crime was himself found murdered after saying he would turn State's evidence.

ours.title: Lynching of Will Thomas
ours.accusation: accused of assaulting Mrs. Eliza Anderson
ours.lead: The lynching of Will Thomas was the hanging of a Black man by a band of about forty armed "regulators" at Tunnel Hill, Georgia, on the evening of March 9, 1888. Thomas was accused of assaulting Mrs. Eliza Anderson, a widow, the day before, and was hanged to a tree after she identified him. Papers across the country carried the Chattanooga dispatches, several stressing that the woman had asked to shoot him and been refused.

ours.title: Lynching of Tom Roof
ours.accusation: accused of said to have assaulted Mrs Joe Morrison at Dlemont Hill
ours.lead: The lynching of Tom Roof took place in Trenton, Georgia, in March 1888, when a mob took a Black man accused of an attempted assault on Mrs. Joseph Morrison from the county jail and hanged him in the public square. Papers across the country carried the story, giving the man's name variously as Roof, Root, Poof and Ruffin. Much of the coverage turned on one wire's claim that the mob "consisted mostly of women."

A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, and papers as far away as Minnesota called him Grimes's murderer.

ours.title: Lynching of Eli Davie
ours.accusation: said to have burned barns
ours.lead: The lynching of Eli Davie was the killing of a Black man, charged with burning a tobacco barn near Fulton, Kentucky, who was taken from a train by masked men at Woodland Mills, Obion County, Tennessee, early on March 15, 1888, and hanged. He was in the custody of a constable who was carrying him to the county jail at Hickman, Kentucky, after an examining trial at Fulton, where open threats to lynch him had been made. A coroner's jury found death at the hands of unknown parties, and a Union City dispatch carried the story from Indiana to California.

ours.title: Killing of Billy Gill
ours.accusation: said to have been a horse thief
ours.lead: The killing of Billy Gill took place in the Indian Territory near Woodward about April 6, 1888, when a party of some two dozen men from southern Kansas pursued Gill, whom they accused of stealing their horses, and shot him dead. No arrest or inquest was reported. Papers from Kansas to Georgia carried the news, treating Gill as a notorious desperado, and one dispatch linked his killers to vigilance committees that meant to execute horse thieves without trial.

ours.title: Lynching of Jeff Curry
ours.accusation: accused of carrying concealed weapons
ours.lead: The lynching of Jeff Curry was the killing of a Black man who was taken from two officers escorting him to jail in Birmingham, Alabama, and shot dead on the road in March 1888. Wire reports placed the killing on Sunday night, March 18, after a dispute with a white man named Powell led to Curry's arrest. Within a week four white men, among them Powell and men who had Curry in charge, were jailed as his murderers, and one paper called it the first time in the state that white men had been held for lynching a Black man.

ours.title: Lynching near Australia Landing, Mississippi (1888)
ours.accusation: accused of shooting and killing another crap-shooter
ours.lead: The lynching near Australia Landing, Mississippi, was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a mob of Black men on a plantation in Bolivar County in late March 1888. He had been accused of killing or wounding a popular man during a quarrel at a plantation ball, and friends of the slain man took him and hanged him to a tree on the Mississippi River levee. Memphis reports carried the story to papers in Kentucky and South Carolina, where one account presented it as the work of a 'Band of Black Ku-Klux'.

ours.title: Lynching of Theo Calloway
ours.accusation: accused of murdering Mitchell Gresham
ours.lead: The lynching of Theo Calloway was the killing of a Black man accused of murdering a white man, Mitchell Gresham, by about 200 armed and masked men who took him from the Lowndes County jail at Hayneville, Alabama, on the night of March 29, 1888, and hanged him in front of the courthouse. A Montgomery dispatch about the lynching ran in papers from Maine to Texas within a week, and the Huntsville Gazette called it "shameful" and urged punishment of the mob. In May, reports of an armed clash between the county sheriff's posse and Black residents traced the trouble to the lynching.

ours.title: Lynching of Slume and Jonninna
ours.accusation: said to have helped murder three prospectors on Wolf creek last June
ours.lead: The lynching of Slume and Jonninna was the hanging of two Kootenai men by a party of white settlers on the east bank of the Flathead River, opposite Demersville in Missoula County, Montana Territory, in March 1888. The settlers accused the two, with a third Kootenai named Antley who escaped, of killing three prospectors on Wolf Creek the previous summer. The hanging set off a scare of a Kootenai uprising, a petition for federal troops and wire coverage across the country.

ours.accusation: said to have helped murder three prospectors on Wolf creek last June
ours.lead: The lynching of Slume and Jonninna was the hanging of two Kootenai men by a party of white settlers on the east bank of the Flathead River, opposite Demersville in Missoula County, Montana Territory, in March 1888. The settlers accused the two, with a third Kootenai named Antley who escaped, of killing three prospectors on Wolf Creek the previous summer. The hanging set off a scare of a Kootenai uprising, a petition for federal troops and wire coverage across the country.

ours.title: Lynching of J. H. Howe
ours.accusation: accused of murdering his wife
ours.lead: The lynching of J. H. Howe took place at Fort Collins, Colorado, on the night of April 4, 1888, when a mob took Howe from the county jail and hanged him from a builders' derrick, hours after his arrest for killing his wife. Wire reports carried the story nationally, and a Denver Republican correspondent reported that doctors, lawyers and clergymen attended and that the town approved.

ours.title: Killing of the "Scar Face" horse-thief gang, 1888
ours.accusation: said to have been horse thieves
ours.lead: The killing of the "Scar Face" horse-thief gang was the pursuit and killing of a band of accused horse thieves by a farmers' vigilance committee in the Indian Territory in April 1888. Reports said that about eight members of the gang died, three of them killed after capture, and that one vigilante was shot dead. Papers nationwide called it a mass lynching; one California paper condemned killing men who had surrendered.

ours.title: Lynching of George Montgomery
ours.accusation: accused of horse stealing
ours.lead: The lynching of George Montgomery was the hanging of a man accused of horse stealing by a vigilance committee of Kansas and No Man's Land settlers at Neutral City, No Man's Land, on Sunday, April 8, 1888. According to an account carried by the Wichita Eagle, Montgomery was captured with four horses said to be stolen, was said to have confessed, and was hanged before seventy-five or one hundred men. Wire specials from Woodward and Oklahoma, Indian Territory, instead told of Kansas farmers hanging four horse thieves and besieging the rest of their band, so the reports disagree on how many died.

ours.title: Killing of the "Scar Face" horse-thief gang, 1888
ours.accusation: said to have been horse thieves

ours.title: Lynching of Jerry Smith
ours.accusation: accused of attempting to assault a white girl
ours.lead: The lynching of Jerry Smith was the hanging of a Black man by a group of men at Tiptonville, Lake county, Tennessee, in April 1888, while he was being held in jail on an accusation of attempted rape. Smith was taken from jail on the morning his case was to come before the court and was found hanging from a tree near the river bank. A Memphis wire carried the news across the country in two lines, and no one was identified as taking part.

ours.lead: The lynching of Isaac and Puss Kirkpatrick was the killing of a Black ("colored") married couple by a mob near Gallatin, Tennessee, about midnight on April 18, 1888, in which the wife was hanged and the husband shot. Puss Kirkpatrick had been suspected of burning a nearby country house, while her husband, who was not suspected, was believed to have been killed because he recognized members of the mob. A wire dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several Northern and Western papers printed it under headlines condemning mob law.

ours.title: Lynching of Hardy Posey
ours.accusation: said to have attempted rape on a white girl aged 15
ours.lead: The lynching of Hardy Posey took place at Bessemer, Alabama, around midnight on April 23, 1888, when masked men took Posey, a Black man accused of attempting to rape a young white girl, from the town marshal and hanged him near the railroad depot. A placard on the body, signed "Bessemer's Best," declared that "our mothers, wives and daughters must and shall be protected." Telegraph reports that Black residents had risen to burn the town in revenge carried the story nationally, though next-day dispatches called the alarm exaggerated.

ours.title: Lynching of Henry Pope
ours.accusation: accused of rape
ours.lead: The lynching of Henry Pope took place at Summerville, Chattooga County, Georgia, on the night of April 30, 1888, when about fifty masked men took Pope, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him from the courthouse banisters. Pope had twice been convicted of assaulting a young white woman, but Governor Gordon had just respited him on evidence that he had been in Alabama that day. Wire briefs called him a "rapist," while an Atlanta dispatch printed in Wheeling and several Northern papers treated the case as the hanging of a probably innocent man.

victims.name: Tom Harris

ours.title: Lynching of Jim Harris
ours.accusation: accused of criminally assaulting Mrs. Simmons
ours.lead: The lynching of Jim Harris was the killing of a Black man at Vicksburg, Mississippi, on the night of April 30, 1888, by men a Mississippi weekly described only as "citizens." Harris had been accused of criminally assaulting a white woman, Mrs. M. Simmons, the night before, and he refused to confess before he was killed. A New Orleans Picayune dispatch carried the case to papers from Georgia to Dakota, while Mississippi papers added that he was hanged at the courthouse door and that officials were criticized for trying to save a white accomplice.

victims.name: George Martin
victims.accusation: Murder of a white man, a deputy marshal

ours.title: Lynching of George Martin
ours.accusation: said to have shot and killed Deputy Marshal Kelly
ours.lead: The lynching of George Martin was the killing of a miner by a mob near Warrior, Jefferson County, Alabama, on the night of May 1, 1888, hours after he was accused of shooting the town's acting marshal, Owen Kelly. Officers tried to move Martin to Birmingham in the caboose of a freight train, but a mob stopped the train, took him from his guards, hanged him to a tree and shot his body. The story ran nationally as a wire item, sometimes naming him Morton.

ours.title: Lynching of John Wright
ours.accusation: accused of killing Budd Vann
ours.lead: The lynching of John Wright took place in St. Helena, Napa County, California, early on May 5, 1888, when a mob of masked men took Wright from the town jail and hanged him from a bridge. Wright had been accused of shooting and killing Budd Vann, a young man of the town, about two weeks earlier, and had been brought to St. Helena for his preliminary examination. A coroner's jury blamed unknown persons, and a Napa County grand jury adjourned without indictments after censuring local officials.

victims.name: Dan Sales
victims.accusation: Attempted rape of an unmarried white woman, a school teacher

ours.title: Lynching of Dan Sale
ours.accusation: accused of attempting to commit an assault upon Miss Smith, school teacher
ours.lead: The lynching of Dan Sale was the hanging of a Black man by a party of about twenty-five men near the village of Danburg, Wilkes County, Georgia, on the night of Sunday, May 6, 1888. Sale, accused of attempting to assault a white schoolteacher, Miss Sallie Smith, had been bound over by a justice of the peace when he was taken from a bailiff and hanged to a tree by the roadside. The story ran as a short Atlanta wire item from Washington to California, and a Savannah dispatch called it the only lynching ever to occur in Wilkes County.

ours.title: Lynching of Thomas Frazier
ours.accusation: said to have shot and killed Joshua H. Coxe, a lumber dealer, after a dispute over liquor
ours.lead: The lynching of Thomas Frazier was the killing of a white man by masked men at Blount's Creek, in Beaufort County, North Carolina, on the night of May 5–6, 1888. Accused of shooting Joshua Cox, a lumberman who had refused him liquor, Frazier was taken from a guarded temporary prison and shot to death where Cox had fallen. Wire reports carried the story nationally, while North Carolina papers disagreed over whether it was justice or a disgrace.

ours.title: Lynching of Morely
ours.accusation: accused of said to have shot James Newbaker and cut off his ear
ours.lead: The lynching of Morely was the hanging, in early May 1888, of a man named Morely or Morley, 'said to be a half-breed', at or near Oak Ridge settlement, Mississippi, after he was accused of waylaying and shooting James Newbaker. The only account was a brief wire dispatch from Vicksburg, which said no particulars of the hanging had been learned. Newspapers from Georgia to Kansas reprinted it within about a week.

ours.title: Lynching of Tom Roney
ours.accusation: said to have poisoned horses
ours.lead: The lynching of Tom Roney was the hanging of a Black farm hand by a mob near Woodburn, in Warren County, Kentucky, in the second week of May 1888. Roney was accused of poisoning the horses of a farmer who had discharged him, and he was taken from the house where he lived and hanged from a tree. A Bowling Green wire report carried the story to papers across the country, and one account called it the first hanging in Warren County in many years.

ours.title: Lynching of Dave Southall
ours.accusation: accused of attempting to kill Mr. Garnet
ours.lead: The lynching of Dave Southall was the killing of a Black man by a large crowd of masked men in Louisiana on the night of Sunday, 13 May 1888, as a deputy sheriff took him through the country after his arrest. Southall had been charged with raising a mob and attempting to kill a man who had challenged his right to vote in Pointe Coupee Parish. A single New Orleans dispatch about the killing ran in at least thirteen papers across the country, under headlines that ranged from 'Lynched in Louisiana' to 'A Case of Poetic Justice'.

ours.title: Lynching of Dandy Hook, Chitwood and two others
ours.accusation: accused of robbery, thievery and murder in the neutral strip and in Southern Kansas
ours.lead: The lynching of Dandy Hook, Chitwood and two others took place on the night of Thursday, May 17, 1888, when a party of vigilantes hanged four men accused of horse stealing in No Man's Land, near Woodward, Indian Territory. Two of the dead were described as known outlaws, while the other two were strangers who protested their innocence to the end. The story ran nationally as a wire item, and one dispatch stated that there was 'no reasonable certainty' that the two strangers were guilty.

ours.title: Lynching of Andrew Grandstaff
ours.accusation: accused of murdering old man Drake and two children
ours.lead: The lynching of Andrew Grandstaff took place at Viroqua, Vernon County, Wisconsin, in the early morning of June 2, 1888, when a mob broke into the county jail, took Grandstaff from the sheriff and hanged him from an oak in front of the court house. Grandstaff had been arrested the night before on a charge of murdering Reuben Drake, Drake's wife and their two grandchildren, and officers said he had confessed. The wire story ran from Pennsylvania to Montana, and Wisconsin weeklies divided over it.

ours.lead: The lynching of Allen Sturgis took place at Thomson, McDuffie County, Georgia, on the night of June 2-3, 1888, when men broke into the town jail, took Sturgis, a young Black man held on burglary charges, and hanged him from an oak beside a road at the edge of town. A coroner's jury found that he died "by parties to us unknown." Local reports called it the first lynching ever in McDuffie County, and brief wire and digest items carried it across the country.

ours.lead: The lynching of Henry Foster was the hanging of a Black hired man by members of a citizen pursuing party near Lansing Switch, six miles east of Longview, Texas, on the night of June 7, 1888. Foster had been accused of attempting to assault an elderly white woman near Friendship three days earlier, and the white Texas press reported his death as deserved punishment.

ours.title: Killing of Bryson near Dardanelle, Arkansas
ours.accusation: said to have attempted criminal assault on the wife of Dock Shinu
ours.lead: The killing of Bryson near Dardanelle, Arkansas, was the shooting of a man pursued by a posse in June 1888, whose body was found in the Arkansas River a few miles below Dardanelle on Sunday, June 10. He had been accused of attempting to assault the wife of a man named Shinn, and a dispatch from Little Rock said Shinn had raised the posse that caught him. The story ran as a brief wire item in papers from Indiana to Nebraska.

ours.title: Lynching of Dennis Williams

ours.lead: The lynching of Dennis Williams took place at Ellaville, Florida, in June 1888, when a mob took Williams, a Black man accused of shooting a mill superintendent, from the men guarding him and killed him. His body was found in the Suwanee River riddled with bullets. The story ran in papers across the country as a short Tallahassee dispatch, which added that Black residents were reported to be planning revenge.

ours.title: Lynching of James Foster
ours.accusation: accused of raping a colored girl eight years old near this city
ours.lead: The lynching of James Foster was the hanging of a Black man, James Foster, by a mounted mob that took him from the jail at Henderson, Kentucky, late on the night of Sunday, June 10, 1888. Foster had been arrested three days earlier on a charge of criminally assaulting the eight-year-old daughter of John Howard, and the mob hanged him from a tree outside the town. The story ran widely as an Evansville wire; a Henderson correspondent added that part of the mob were Black men and that it nearly lynched a second prisoner.

ours.title: Lynching of Robert Robertson
ours.accusation: accused of killing an innocent bystander in a row over a sporting woman
ours.lead: The lynching of Robert Robertson was the hanging of a Black private of the Twenty-fifth Infantry by masked men at Sun River, Montana Territory, about midnight on June 10–11, 1888. Robertson, called Robinson in many reports, was accused of fatally shooting Charles McGuire, a Sun River freighter, and was taken from a deputy at the Sun River jail. A judge sitting at Great Falls charged the grand jury against the lynchers, whom the grand jury could not identify.

ours.title: Lynching of Schenck (Monarch, Colorado)
ours.accusation: accused of shooting Geo. Davis in a saloon row
ours.lead: The lynching of Schenck was the hanging of a one-legged gambler by a mob at Monarch, Colorado, on the night of June 13, 1888, after he was accused of shooting two men in a saloon row. The mob hanged him to a telegraph pole, and the dispatch reported that friends of the dead men were gathering and that more trouble was feared. The story reached papers across the country as one short wire item from Salida and was then condensed into weekly news digests.

ours.title: Lynching of Washington Ives
ours.accusation: said to have attempted to assault a young lady
ours.lead: The lynching of Washington Ives was the hanging of a Black man near Natchez, Mississippi, on the night of June 16, 1888, after he was accused of attempting to assault a young woman. His body was found the next morning hanging from a tree with a card warning against rape, and no one was reported arrested. The Natchez wire report ran in papers from New York to Georgia, and the case later appeared on a year-end list of the "Victims of Judge Lynch."

ours.title: Lynching of William Stokes
ours.accusation: said to have broken into a white employer's house with intent other than robbery and forced entry into a colored tenant's house, where assault was suspected
ours.lead: The lynching of William Stokes was the killing of a Black farm laborer who was shot dead after being taken from a constable's custody near Marmora, Dinwiddie County, Virginia, in June 1888. Stokes had been arrested on a charge arising from alleged entries into houses on the farm where he had worked, and his body was found in a road a short distance from where he had been held. A coroner's jury found that he had been shot by persons unknown, and in August a Dinwiddie grand jury dismissed the matter for lack of evidence. Virginia papers treated the case as a lynching carried out with such secrecy that no one was ever suspected.

ours.title: Lynching of Frank Davis
ours.accusation: accused of attempted rape of a young girl
ours.lead: The lynching of Frank Davis was the hanging of a Black man by masked men in the court-house yard at Tupelo, Mississippi, early on June 19, 1888. Davis, charged with an attempted rape of a girl at Saltillo, was taken from the Lee County jail after the lynchers seized Sheriff Long. Memphis and Mississippi papers carried the story under the headline "A Negro Rapist Lynched," and later counted it among three lynchings in the state in one week.

ours.lead: The lynching of Ned Clark was the shooting of a Black man, described in the press as "colored," by the men holding him prisoner in Worth County, Georgia, reported on June 26, 1888. Clark had been charged with attempting to assault a thirteen-year-old girl, and his captors said he was shot while trying to escape as they took him toward Irwin County; his body was found with nineteen bullets in it. The account, which came from a single dispatch out of Albany, ran in papers across the country and put Clark's name on a year-end list of the "Victims of Judge Lynch."

ours.title: Lynching of William Moore
ours.accusation: accused of assaulting Mary A. Bingardiner at Nation, Ills., Saturday night
ours.lead: The lynching of William Moore took place early on June 26, 1888, when a mob of armed men broke into the jail at Charleston, Coles County, Illinois, and hanged Moore, a Black man from Mattoon, from the water tank near the depot. He had been accused of assaulting a young white woman, Mary A. Bumgardner, and was being held for the grand jury. Within days, dispatches from her home district called her of bad repute and Moore innocent, and in October nine men were indicted.

ours.title: Lynching of Wallace Mitchell
ours.accusation: accused of murder
ours.lead: The lynching of Wallace Mitchell took place at Syracuse, Hamilton County, Kansas, early on June 27, 1888, when a crowd of a hundred or more men took him from jail and hanged him for the murder of a twelve-year-old boy, Oscar Johnson. The men got in after the sheriff fled with the keys and hanged Mitchell from a telegraph pole where the killing had occurred. Many papers reported it as one of four Kansas lynchings in twenty-four hours.

ours.title: Lynching of John Risbee and Wyley Lee
ours.accusation: accused of shooting the marshal and a deputy while trying to escape
ours.lead: The lynching of John Risbee and Wyley Lee took place at Chetopa, Kansas, in the early morning of June 27, 1888, when a mob of 200 to 300 men took the two Black men from a sheriff's guard and hanged them from a newspaper office window. The two had been accused of shooting the town marshal and his deputy, both of whom were later reported alive. Papers noted it chiefly for a coroner's jury of four white and eight Black men that split over naming the mob.

The two had been accused of shooting the town marshal and his deputy, both of whom were later reported alive. Papers noted it chiefly for a coroner's jury of four white and eight Black men that split over naming the mob.

ours.title: Lynching of Chubb McCarthy
ours.accusation: accused of murdering Mike Dorsey
ours.lead: The lynching of Chubb McCarthy took place early on 28 June 1888, when a mob took McCarthy, accused of murdering Mike Dorsey, from the jail at Minneapolis, Kansas, and hanged him from a bridge over the Solomon River. The mob held the sheriff and city marshal under guard while it worked, and the body was found hanging at 7 a.m. Newspapers across the country reported it as the last of four lynchings in Kansas within twenty-four hours, which the wire report linked to the state's death-penalty law.

ours.title: Lynching of Calvin Moody

ours.lead: The lynching of Calvin Moody was the hanging of a Black man accused of murdering his wife, carried out by a mob of about 200 Black men at Moulton, Lawrence County, Alabama, on the night of July 1, 1888, by most accounts. The mob overpowered the sheriff and a guard, took Moody from the jail, and hanged him from a tree outside town after he reportedly confessed. Wire reports printed across the country called it the first lynching in Alabama of a Black man by members of his own race.

ours.lead: The lynching of Robert Bryan took place on the evening of July 6, 1888, on the outskirts of Henderson, Kentucky, when about fifty masked men took the Black youth of about sixteen from the men conveying him to jail and hanged him to a tree. Bryan had been accused of stabbing to death Riley Hancock, a nineteen-year-old white man, near Smith's Mills earlier that day. A Nashville American dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and the Hopkinsville South Kentuckian treated it as the latest in a run of mob actions at Henderson.

According to a syndicated news digest, Staples was lynched after being accused of assaulting the seventeen-year-old daughter of Hardy McCoy, described as a wealthy planter. The episode is known only from that one sentence, which several Midwestern weeklies printed in the following days.

Smith had been accused of assaulting an elderly white woman near New River Bridge in Pulaski County the week before. Early wire reports said he had already been hanged near the scene, and Virginia papers printed conflicting versions before the Wytheville account appeared.

ours.lead: The killing of Jim Torney was the reported killing of a Black farm laborer by a crowd of white men near Pell City, Alabama, in July 1888, after he eloped with Maude Broyles, the sixteen-year-old white daughter of his employer. Birmingham dispatches said the pursuers recovered the girl and were believed to have killed Torney and thrown his body into the Coosa River, though no report said a body was found. The story broke the same week as the lynching of Frank Stone at Pell City, and a national news digest joined the two cases in a single sentence.

ours.title: Lynching of Frank Stone
ours.accusation: accused of an outrage on Mrs. Orr, white
ours.lead: The lynching of Frank Stone took place on the evening of July 13, 1888, near Pell City, Alabama, when a crowd of about fifty white men hanged Stone, a Black man, to a tree and riddled his body with bullets. Stone had been accused the day before of attempting to assault Mrs. Orr, a white woman, and was lynched within hours of his capture. Birmingham dispatches carried the story to papers in Memphis, Louisville, Atlanta and Ohio, and a one-line summary ran in Northern weeklies.

ours.title: Lynching of John Humphreys
ours.accusation: accused of brutally assaulting a twelve-year-old girl
ours.lead: The lynching of John Humphreys was the killing of a Black man by masked men who broke into the county jail at Asheville, North Carolina, early on Sunday, July 15, 1888, and hanged him from a tree. Humphreys had been arrested the night before, accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old white girl, and the mob spent about an hour battering apart the steel cage that held him. The story ran by wire across the country, and the Charlotte Democrat called it "the first lynching known in Western North Carolina."

ours.title: Lynching of Jack Walker
ours.accusation: said to have struck the wife of German in a quarrel over a horse
ours.lead: The lynching of Jack Walker was the killing of a Black man at or near Brenham, Texas, on July 23, 1888. A wire report said he was lynched because he struck the wife of a German in a quarrel over a horse, and a Texas paper reported that several German citizens had been arrested as participants. Outside Texas the episode reached readers as a single line in weekly news digests printed in Wisconsin, Dakota and Chicago.

ours.title: Killing of Levi Lally
ours.lead: The killing of Levi Lally was the fatal shooting of a farmer at his house near Montevallo, Alabama, on the night of Saturday, July 21, 1888, by two white men and a Black man who had called him outside. Lally died the next day, and warrants were issued on suspicion against men with whom he had quarrelled over work. The case reached distant papers through a single Montgomery dispatch, and a moonshiner killing in Bibb County, reported about ten days later, bore some resemblance to it.

ours.title: Lynching of Bruce Younger
ours.accusation: said to have committed an assault upon Mrs. Robert Dodge
ours.lead: The lynching of Bruce Younger took place about midnight on July 26, 1888, at Halifax Court-House, Virginia, when a party of armed horsemen took Younger, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him from a footbridge. Younger had been arrested that morning, accused of assaulting Mrs. Robert Dodd, a white woman near Meadsville. Virginia papers described it as the first lynching ever carried out in Halifax County, and correspondents there defended it as justified.

ours.title: Lynching of Eli Bryant
ours.accusation: said to have made an indecent assault upon a respectable white lady
ours.lead: The lynching of Eli Bryant was the hanging of a Black man by a white mob at Harges Station, near Starkville, Mississippi, on July 27, 1888. Bryant had been accused of assaulting a white woman, and papers reported that a crowd of 500 to 800 men hanged him after he was caught. The story went out by wire and ran in Southern, Northern and Mississippi papers over the next three weeks, usually presenting his guilt as settled.

ours.title: Lynching of L. S. Elmer
ours.accusation: accused of shooting Mollie out of jealousy
ours.lead: The lynching of L. S. Elmer took place early on July 27, 1888, at Wahpeton, Dakota Territory, when a masked mob took the deputy sheriff from the Richland County jail and hanged him from the bridge over the Bois des Sioux River. Elmer was accused of having shot Mollie Korbel, a domestic in the sheriff's household, two days earlier. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown; the local paper hailed the hanging as justice, and wire reports spread it nationally, stressing that the sheriff would not fire on the mob.

ours.accusation: accused of murder
ours.lead: The lynching of W. H. Handley took place on the night of July 31, 1888, when a mob of about fifty armed men broke into the jail at Carthage, Smith County, Tennessee, took out Handley, and hanged him to a tree. Handley, about 23, was awaiting trial, set for the next day, on a charge of killing a deputy sheriff the previous September. The papers noted the resistance of the sheriff and his posse, who exchanged about thirty shots with the mob before it reached the prisoner.

ours.title: Lynching of Fremont Emmons
ours.accusation: accused of stabbing Bertha Schults, who had refused his proposal of marriage
ours.lead: The lynching of Fremont Emmons took place at Pawnee City, Nebraska, in the early hours of July 31, 1888, when a mob took Emmons from deputies guarding him in the court house and hanged him from a railroad bridge. Emmons, a hotel cook, was charged with stabbing to death Bertha Schultz, who worked at the same hotel, after she refused to marry him. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown, and Nebraska papers called this lynching justified while warning against mobs in general.

ours.title: Henderson County abduction of an unknown white man (1888)
ours.accusation: said to have made an alleged assault upon a negro woman
ours.lead: The Henderson County abduction of an unknown white man was an episode in Henderson County, North Carolina, in early August 1888, in which five Black men reportedly beat a white man senseless and carried him off with a rope. The man was not seen again, five men were jailed at Hendersonville, and the white press reported the case as a lynching "by negroes." A body later seen in the French Broad River near Asheville was supposed to be his, but it was never recovered.

ours.title: Lynching of Amos Miller
ours.accusation: accused of assaulting Mrs. Scott
ours.lead: The lynching of Amos Miller was the hanging of a Black man accused of assaulting Mrs. Scott, a white woman of Maury County, Tennessee, by an armed mob that seized him in the court room at Franklin, Williamson County, on August 10, 1888. About fifty unmasked men took Miller while his lawyers sought a delay in his trial and hanged him from a railing of the court house in the presence of the court. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of unknown parties.

ours.title: Lynching of Bob Broom
ours.accusation: said to have shot Dr. I W. Halliday
ours.lead: The lynching of Bob Broom was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of more than 200 men at Utica, Hinds County, Mississippi, on August 13, 1888. Broom had been jailed the night before, accused of leading a party of Black men who shot Dr. L. W. Holliday dead and wounded two other white men after a quarrel over the sidewalk. The story ran across the country, and a month later papers reported that a second accused man, Curtis Shortney, had been taken from a train and was supposed lynched.

ours.title: Lynching of Noah Griffin
ours.accusation: accused of insulting a white woman
ours.lead: The lynching of Noah Griffin was the shooting of a Black man by forty masked men at Ocheeshee, Calhoun County, Florida, on Wednesday, August 15, 1888. Griffin had been accused of writing an insulting note to a young white woman, for which a group of white men had already whipped him and ordered him out of the county. The killing reached papers across the country through a single Apalachicola dispatch, and two papers, in Kansas and Minnesota, printed comments condemning it.

ours.title: Lynching of two prisoners at Sylvaren, Mississippi
ours.accusation: accused of killing a white man named Lee
ours.lead: The lynching of two prisoners at Sylvaren, Mississippi, was the shooting of two Black men in a Smith County jail by a mob in mid-August 1888. The two were among four Black prisoners under arrest, accused of killing a white man named Lee, and were shot dead inside the jail. A brief New Orleans dispatch carried the story to papers from New York and Maine to Dakota, and a Leavenworth, Kansas, paper used it in a campaign appeal against the Democratic party.

ours.title: Lynching of Billy Cole
ours.accusation: accused of shooting two men
ours.lead: The lynching of Billy Cole was the hanging of William "Billy" Cole, accused of shooting two men at a dance, by twelve masked men who took him from the lockup at Guide Rock, Nebraska, early on August 20, 1888. He was hanged from a railroad bridge while both men he had wounded were reported alive, and the lynchers were not identified. Wire reports carried the story nationally the next day, and some Nebraska editors treated it lightly.

ours.title: Bayou Martin raid
ours.lead: The Bayou Martin raid was an armed attack in August 1888 in which about 250 white men surprised Albert Narcisse, a Black man, and his brother in a field on Bayou Martin, nine miles from St. Martinsville, Louisiana, and fired on them after they fled to Narcisse's house. Narcisse and a ten-year-old boy were shot, the two men were captured, and the whites reported finding thirty new guns in the cabin. The main dispatch said the captives' fate was unknown, while one condensed version said Narcisse and his son had been fatally shot. Northern papers carried the report under headlines about Louisiana "race troubles" and whites "enraged" at Black residents arming themselves.

ours.lead: The lynching of Graves was the hanging of a 16-year-old Black boy by a mob near Brownstown, Sevier County, Arkansas, late on the night of Friday, August 24, 1888. He had been accused of assaulting the five-year-old daughter of a white farmer, and the mob took him from the officers who held him. A brief dispatch from Little Rock carried the news to papers across the country, and later summaries gave a different charge.

ours.title: Lynching of Harrison Spencer
ours.lead: The lynching of Harrison Spencer was the abduction and killing of a Black farmer and local politician near Longview, Gregg County, Texas, in late August 1888 by a masked band that took him from his home at night. His body was found several days later hanging from a tree on Harris Creek, shot, whipped and mutilated. Papers tied the killing to his break with the Union Labor party, and the case was read into a United States Senate debate as an example of political murder in Texas.

ours.accusation: accused of criminally assaulting three women of that place
ours.lead: The lynching of Pony Poe was the hanging of a Black man by a mob of about 300 men near Bellefontaine, Webster County, Mississippi, in late August 1888. Poe, accused of assaulting three women, was taken from a sheriff's posse on the way to jail and hanged at the scene of the alleged crime. Newspapers across the country carried the story, many noting that he was a former teacher, a leader of the county's Black residents and a recent candidate for public office.

ours.accusation: accused of assaulting a white girl
ours.lead: The lynching of Archer Cook was the killing of a Black man, about 22, whom armed and masked men took from the Prince Edward County jail at Farmville, Virginia, early on August 31, 1888, and hanged and shot. Cook had been jailed for months awaiting trial on a charge of assaulting a young white woman, Lizzie Frank. Wire items carried the news across the Midwest and the Dakotas, and a Leavenworth, Kansas, weekly addressed to Black readers urged them to arm and guard the jails.

ours.title: Lynching of Henry Tanner, John Tanner and Alonzo Smith
ours.accusation: accused of murder of 'Squire Grissom (Henry and John Tanner); accused of burglary and arson (Alonzo Smith)
ours.lead: The lynching of Henry Tanner, John Tanner and Alonzo Smith was the hanging of three Black prisoners by a masked crowd that took them from the jail at Oxford, Granville County, North Carolina, at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, September 2, 1888. The Tanners, father and son, were charged with murdering an elderly Black man, Squire Grissom, and Smith with arson or burglary and arson. A Raleigh dispatch called it a lynching "such as was never before recorded in the history of the State."

ours.title: Lynching of John Baker
ours.lead: The lynching of John Baker was the reported hanging of a farm hand by his fellow threshing workers on the farm of a man named Weeks near Guide Rock, in Webster County, Nebraska, on September 1, 1888. Baker was accused of feeding the boy who cut bands on the crew into the threshing machine after the boy accidentally cut his hand, and the other hands hanged him from the machine's straw carrier. The story ran nationally under an "Agenda, Kan." dateline, and one Kansas editor called it a fabrication that had fooled the Associated Press.

ours.title: Lynching of William Lewis
ours.lead: The lynching of William Lewis was the hanging of a Black man by unknown persons near Durant, Mississippi, whose body was found on a tree on the morning of September 4, 1888. No cause was assigned and the perpetrators were not identified. The case reached readers only as a brief wire item, printed in Savannah and in several Northern papers the next day.

ours.title: Lynching of Sherman Farrior
ours.accusation: said to have committed an outrage on an aged white woman
ours.lead: The lynching of Sherman Farrior took place in Whiteville, Columbus County, North Carolina, on the night of September 12, 1888, when a body of a hundred or more men took Farrior, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from an oak tree. Farrior was awaiting trial on a charge of outraging an aged white woman. North Carolina papers counted the hanging as the thirteenth lynching in the state that year, and reports differed on whether the mob was made up of masked men of unstated race or of Black men.

ours.title: Breaux Bridge night raid
ours.lead: The Breaux Bridge night raid was an attack on the night of September 14, 1888, in which four or five armed men went to Black cabins near Breaux Bridge, Louisiana, killed a Black woman, whipped a Black man, and sexually assaulted a Black woman. Five men were arrested; one, Sam Polk, turned state's witness and named Vilmont Hollier as the man who fired, and two were held without bail. The killing was carried by wire across the country and was cited in the United States Senate as political violence.

ours.title: Lynching of Wise (Dakota, 1888)
ours.accusation: accused of horse stealing
ours.lead: The lynching of Wise was the hanging of an accused horse thief by settlers in the Turtle Mountains of Dakota on Wednesday, September 12, 1888. According to accounts relayed from Bismarck, several settlers who had missed horses overtook him on his way to Manitoba, disarmed him, and hanged him from the nearest tree. Papers across the country carried the story because the dead man was said to have once been a prominent citizen of Wyoming mentioned for its legislature.

ours.title: Lynching of Jean Pierre Salet and Didaere
ours.accusation: said to have used incendiary language
ours.lead: The lynching of Jean Pierre Salet and Didaere was the killing of two Black men by a crowd of armed men at Ville Platte Prairie, near Opelousas in St. Landry Parish, Louisiana, on September 16, 1888. The men were taken from their homes, led a short distance away and shot with buckshot, reportedly because of "incendiary language" they had used. A short Opelousas dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, under headlines that gave the victims' speech as the cause of their deaths.

ours.title: Lynching of Lewis Davis
ours.accusation: accused of murdering David Miller
ours.lead: The lynching of Lewis Davis was the hanging of a jailed prisoner by a masked mob in Crawford County, Missouri, early on Sunday, September 23, 1888. Davis, awaiting trial for the murder of his neighbor David Miller, was taken from jail and hanged over the grave of Pat Wallace, whom a mob had lynched two years before. The papers dwelt on his fight in his cell, and the judge ordered a special grand jury.

ours.title: Lynching of Sam Cornwall
ours.accusation: said to have quarreled with a white man, Tom Smith; peace warrant issued against him
ours.lead: The lynching of Sam Cornwall was the shooting death of a Black prisoner on a public road in Chester County, South Carolina, in the early morning of September 29 or 30, 1888, while he was in a constable's custody on a peace warrant. His guard said they were fired on from ambush and fled, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of parties unknown. Papers from New York to Texas carried the story, several of them blaming the officers who had left him.

rows.name: Aaron Bean

ours.title: Lynching of Aaron Bean
ours.accusation: accused of attempting to assault a girl
ours.lead: The lynching of Aaron Bean took place near Jasper, Texas, on Wednesday, October 3, 1888, when a mob took Bean, a Black man, from officers on the road to jail and shot him to death. Bean had been accused of accosting the young daughter of a Magnolia Springs farmer while she was riding and dragging her from her saddle. The killing was known outside Texas through a single Galveston wire dispatch, which several papers printed under headlines approving of it.

victims.accusation: Shooting at a white man, a doctor, and shooting at a posse

ours.title: Lynching of John Kirkland
ours.lead: The lynching of John Kirkland was the killing of a prisoner by masked men near the jail at Nashville, Arkansas, on the night of October 8, 1888. Kirkland, accused of firing on a local physician, was taken from a constable and shot to death. Brief wire dispatches carried the story to papers in Dakota Territory and Kansas.

ours.title: Lynching of Hickman
ours.accusation: said to have shot and killed J. G. Booth
ours.lead: The lynching of Hickman was the killing of a man named Hickman by a mob of about seventy-five men at Boston, Colorado, in early October 1888. Hickman was accused of having shot and killed J. C. Booth, a man who had been visiting the woman Hickman lived with, and the mob took him from his house within hours and hanged him. The story reached the national press as a brief Trinidad dispatch and was reprinted in papers from Georgia to Dakota over the following two weeks.

ours.title: Lynching of Nat Nathaniel
ours.accusation: accused of killing Isaac Van Dorn
ours.lead: The lynching of Nat Nathaniel was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd near Brazoria, Texas, in October 1888, after he was accused of shooting Isaac Van Dorn, a plantation engineer. Citizens captured Nathaniel at Wharton, but on the road to the Brazoria jail, about five miles from Brazoria, a crowd took him from his captors and hanged him. The wire story dwelt less on the hanging than on reported threats of retaliation by Black residents, and headlines spoke of a feared race war.

ours.title: Pittsville church shooting
ours.lead: The Pittsville church shooting was an attack in October 1888 in which a crowd of armed young white men rode up to a Black church at Pittsville, in Fort Bend County, Texas, called the congregation out and fired into it. Lamar Johnson was killed and Taylor Randon was wounded. The Galveston News called it a political assassination and blamed the Jay Bird Club, a new Democratic organization, while a leading Fort Bend Democrat denied that politics played any part.

ours.title: Lynching of Bill Johnson
ours.accusation: said to have outraged Mrs. Newman
ours.lead: The lynching of Bill Johnson took place near Cochran, Georgia, on Saturday, October 13, 1888, when a crowd of men hanged Johnson, a Black farm hand, from a tree a mile from town and riddled his body with bullets. Johnson had been accused of outraging the wife of the farmer who employed him, and the crowd left a placard on his body reading "Our women must and shall be protected." A wire dispatch carried the story to papers across the country within two days.

ours.title: Lynching of Joe Joiner
ours.accusation: accused of attempted assault upon a white girl
ours.lead: The lynching of Joe Joiner took place at Hutto, Texas, near Taylor and Round Rock, in mid-October 1888, when a mob of masked men hanged Joiner, a Black man, to a tree. Joiner had been accused of attempting to assault a young white girl and had been captured and placed in the hands of the sheriff or officers. A Taylor dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, one of which headlined it "A Negro Brute Hanged by a Mob."

ours.title: Lynching of Lewis Edwards
ours.accusation: said to have murdered Robert J. Smith in January 1886
ours.lead: The lynching of Lewis Edwards was the killing of a Black prisoner by masked men in the county jail at Jesup, Wayne County, Georgia, at about 3 a.m. on October 15, 1888. Edwards had been brought back from confinement to stand a new trial for the 1886 killing of a Jesup hotel proprietor when the men overpowered his guards and shot him in his cell. A coroner's jury attributed his death to an unknown unlawful mob, and the Atlanta Constitution's correspondent called it the first lynching on record in the county.

ours.title: Lynching of F. W. Adams and Charles Lutzier
ours.accusation: said to have maliciously burned a ranchman's house and slaughtered game out of season
ours.lead: The lynching of F. W. Adams and "Dutchy" was the hanging of two hunters by masked settlers on the Snake River in Carbon County, Wyoming Territory, in October 1888. Accused of slaughtering elk and deer for their hides and of burning a ranchman's house, the two were taken from a guarded adobe hut and hanged from a tree. Later reports of mutilation, fleeing witnesses and freed suspects led Wyoming papers to call it "one of the most atrocious outrages ever committed in Wyoming territory."

ours.title: Lynching of Sam Smith
ours.accusation: accused of raping the wife of a section boss
ours.lead: The lynching of Sam Smith took place near Forney, Texas, on October 25, 1888, when armed and masked men took Smith, a Black man accused of rape, from officers taking him to jail at Kaufman and hanged and shot him. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of unknown persons, and Black residents refused to let him be buried in their graveyard. Texas papers noted the speed of the killing, which came less than a day after the alleged crime.

ours.title: Lynching of Henry Jones
ours.accusation: accused of murder
ours.lead: The lynching of Henry Jones took place near Woodland Mills, in Obion County, Tennessee, on the night of October 26, 1888, when a mob killed Jones, a Black man. A Nashville wire dispatch said he had murdered a white man, while a Kentucky weekly, the Hickman Courier, said he had shot at a man and wounded his horse, and that he was taken from officers and hanged. The two-sentence wire item ran in papers from Virginia to Washington Territory, and no report of an inquest or arrests appears in the coverage.

ours.title: Lynching of Thomas Sayers
ours.accusation: accused of robbery and killing of two white travellers
ours.lead: The lynching of Thomas Sayers took place near Bramwell, Mercer County, West Virginia, around the beginning of November 1888, when a mob took Sayers, a Black man accused of leading a highway robbery, from officers taking him to jail and hanged him from a tree. He had been held for the grand jury after an attack on four white produce sellers in which two were shot. A Post-Dispatch wire carried the news nationally under headlines such as "Negro Murderer Lynched," though reports differed on the date, on whether the robbery victims died, and on how many men were lynched.

ours.title: Lynching of Macum Marshall
ours.accusation: accused of assaulting a white woman
ours.lead: The lynching of Macum Marshall was the killing of a Black man by a posse of armed men near Blackshear, Georgia, on November 2, 1888. Marshall was accused of raping Mrs. Henry Howard, a farmer's wife, in her home that morning, and was captured in a nearby swamp and lynched the same day. The story reached readers in Savannah, Kentucky and California as a short wire item.

ours.title: Lynching of Archibald Pelon
ours.accusation: accused of assault on an old lady
ours.lead: The lynching of Archibald Pelon took place at Grayling, Michigan, in the early hours of November 7, 1888, when masked men took him from the sheriff and hanged him from a beam between two trees. Pelon had been arrested for allegedly assaulting two women near Beaver Creek, and no arrests for his killing were reported. The fullest wire dispatch noted that Michigan had seen no lynching in fifteen years.

ours.title: Lynching of Judson Cason
ours.accusation: said to have cut John L. Bryan with a knife
ours.lead: The lynching of Judson Cason was the killing of a Black man, accused of cutting John L. Bryan, who was seized near Lloyd's Station, Jefferson County, Florida, on election day, November 6, 1888, and found dead in the Miccosukie Sinks. A coroner's jury named eight men, among them Bryan, and a grand jury reportedly indicted four while Bryan remained a fugitive. Northern papers took particular notice because Bryan was the son of the writer Mary E. Bryan, who said her son thought he was doing right.

ours.title: Lynching of Davis Sabini
ours.accusation: said to have shot Richard Holt because Holt would not lend him money
ours.lead: The lynching of Davis Sabini was the hanging of a 22-year-old Italian man by residents of Cortez, Nevada, in November 1888, after he was accused of fatally shooting Richard "Dick" Holt in a quarrel over a loan. The men involved told a deputy sheriff that Sabini had hanged himself, and a coroner's jury returned a verdict of suicide that the Elko Independent openly doubted. The story ran as a brief wire item in papers across the country, and in Cortez it led the town's Italian residents to threaten revenge.

ours.title: Lynching of Jim Smith
ours.accusation: said to have made an insulting proposal to a white farmer's wife
ours.lead: The lynching of Jim Smith was the killing of a Black man by a mob of white men in Crittenden County, Arkansas, in late November 1888. Smith, accused of an offense against a white farmer's wife, was taken from a deputy sheriff on the way to jail at Marion and shot. The case reached readers only through brief wire items in papers outside Arkansas.

ours.accusation: accused of assaulting a young white girl
ours.lead: The 1888 Donaldsonville lynching was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a crowd that took him from a jailer near Donaldsonville, Louisiana, in mid-November 1888, after he was accused of assaulting an eleven-year-old white girl on a nearby plantation. The account, a special dispatch to the New Orleans Times-Democrat, was reprinted across the country over the next nine days under headlines such as "A Wretch Lynched" and "Black Flend Lynched."

ours.title: Killing of Oscar Carmichael
ours.lead: The killing of Oscar Carmichael was the shooting of an escaped Georgia convict by a posse at his wife's house in or near Henry County, Georgia, on the night of Friday, November 16, 1888, hours after he was accused of killing his guard, W. J. Gresham, near Griffin. Reports said the posse "riddled" him with shot or bullets, and differed on whether he died in an exchange of fire or was fired on as he approached the house. A Griffin wire story about the guard's death and the bloodhound chase ran in papers from Minnesota to Texas under headlines such as "Speedy Vengeance Overtakes a Prisoner Who Murdered His Guard."

ours.title: Lynching of Wilson Arnold
ours.accusation: accused of the murder of Captain Robert Johnson
ours.lead: The lynching of Wilson Arnold was the killing of a Black man, also named in the papers as Wilkes or Wilks Arnold, who was taken from the jail at Yazoo City, Mississippi, by an armed mob on November 19, 1888, and hanged. Arnold had surrendered to the sheriff about a week earlier after shooting Captain Robert Johnson, a white planter, near Satartia, a killing he said was in self-defense. A Yazoo County grand jury later reported that it could not identify any of the lynchers, although about fifteen were said to be known.

ours.title: Lynching of Jack Jones
ours.accusation: accused of assaulting white women
ours.lead: The lynching of Jack Jones was the hanging of a Black man by a mob at or near Rockwood, Tennessee, reported as having taken place on Thursday, November 22, 1888. Jones was accused of assaulting, or attempting to assault, two women who lived near Rockwood. The story travelled only as one-sentence telegraph and column items, which ran in papers from New York and New Jersey to Mississippi and Louisiana over the following week.

ours.accusation: accused of criminal assault on a young girl
ours.lead: The lynching of Jerry Taylor was the killing of a Black man in St. Helena Parish, Louisiana, on the night of November 22, 1888. He was accused of criminally assaulting the thirteen-year-old daughter of J. C. Williams. The case reached the press only as one-sentence wire and digest items, which ran in papers from Washington and New York to Minnesota, Wisconsin, Iowa and Dakota over the following week.

ours.title: Lynching of Tim Smith and John Coleman
ours.accusation: said to have insulted white ladies and threatened citizens
ours.lead: The lynching of Tim Smith and John Coleman took place on the night of Tuesday, November 27, 1888, when white men took the two Black men from a convict stockade near Danburg, Wilkes County, Georgia, and, by most accounts, drowned them in the Broad River. The same party whipped two other Black people, Hulda or Huldah Smith and a male relative. Dispatches called it a "race war" arising from a cotton dispute and an alleged insult to a white woman, and the Augusta Chronicle denounced it as "crimes against civilization and Christianity."

ours.lead: The lynching of Van Canady was the hanging of a young Black man, also called John Carson, by a crowd that took him from the jail at Shelby, North Carolina, just after midnight on December 1-2, 1888. Canady had been accused of murdering James Philbeck, a white farmer, and was reported to have confessed the day before. A coroner's jury found that he died "at the hands of parties unknown", and the story ran as a brief across the country, while North Carolina papers called the lynching just punishment.

ours.title: Lynching of George Witherell
ours.accusation: accused of murder
ours.lead: The lynching of George Witherell took place at Canon City, Colorado, early on December 4, 1888, when armed men broke into the jail, shot him and hanged him from a pole. Witherell had been returned to Canon City the day before to stand trial for the murder of a freighter, Charles McCain. The Associated Press account ran nationwide, dwelling on his fight in the cell and the other killings he was accused of.

Taylor had been arrested as a suspect in the ambush killing of R. N. Stegall on a road below Harrisonburg a few days earlier. A Times-Democrat dispatch from Natchez carried the story to papers across the country, some of which set it against the news from Birmingham, Alabama, where a sheriff had defended his jail against a mob.

ours.title: Killing of Adam Golden
ours.lead: The killing of Adam Golden occurred on a Monday night in December 1888, when a masked mob stoning the house of Jennie Maddox, seven miles north of Buchanan in Haralson County, Georgia, beat and shot to death Golden, a Black man who had intervened. Five white men and two Black men were jailed for the murder and three white women were held for taking part. The story ran on the telegraph across the country, where it appeared beside reports of White Cap outrages and under headlines such as "Killed for His Interference."

ours.title: Lynching of an unnamed gambler near Cumberland Gap, Tennessee
ours.accusation: said to have shot and fatally wounded Captain Dunnavant
ours.lead: The lynching of an unnamed gambler near Cumberland Gap, Tennessee, took place in mid-December 1888, when a mob took a Black man from the posse that had arrested him and hanged him from a tree. He was accused of leading an armed party that fired on a railroad contractor's camp after laborers had driven him away. The story ran as a short wire item in papers across the country, and later weekly digests misreported it as the lynching of a man who had fatally wounded a "Captain Dunnavant" near Chattanooga.

ours.title: Wahalak race riot
ours.accusation: said to have taken part in an ambush of white men
ours.lead: The Wahalak race riot was an armed clash near Wahalak, Kemper County, Mississippi, on December 16, 1888, in which Black men at the home of a Black man named Maury fired on a white posse, followed by a white manhunt in which Black homes were burned. ours.title: Death of an unidentified man in the Boston Mountains, Arkansas (1888)
ours.lead: In February 1888 two hunters found the body of an unidentified, heavily armed man in the Boston Mountains of Arkansas, near a still where a revenue collector had killed its owner the previous fall. No marks showed how he died, but newspapers supposed he was a detective gathering evidence against illicit distilling and headlined the death "Murdered by Moonshiners."

ours.title: Lynching of Franklin Baker
ours.accusation: accused of shooting two young men (N. B. Mcconnell and John Morrison)
ours.lead: The lynching of Franklin Baker was the hanging of a Colorado homesteader by a mob at Cheyenne Wells in April 1888, after he was arrested for shooting two land seekers who crossed his claim. Officers were moving him toward Denver when the mob, put at fifty men, took him and hanged him to a railroad coal chute. The case ran in papers from Washington to California, first as a shooting and a promised lynching, then as brief notices of the hanging.

ours.title: Lynching of Schenck (Monarch, Colorado)
ours.accusation: accused of shooting Geo. Davis in a saloon row
ours.lead: The lynching of Schenck was the hanging of a one-legged gambler by a mob at Monarch, Colorado, on the night of June 13, 1888, after he was accused of shooting two men in a saloon row. The mob hanged him to a telegraph pole, and the dispatch reported that friends of the dead men were gathering and that more trouble was feared. The story reached papers across the country as one short wire item from Salida and was then condensed into weekly news digests.

ours.title: Lynching of Theo Calloway
ours.accusation: accused of murdering Mitchell Gresham
ours.lead: The lynching of Theo Calloway was the killing of a Black man accused of murdering a white man, Mitchell Gresham, by about 200 armed and masked men who took him from the Lowndes County jail at Hayneville, Alabama, on the night of March 29, 1888, and hanged him in front of the courthouse. A Montgomery dispatch about the lynching ran in papers from Maine to Texas within a week, and the Huntsville Gazette called it "shameful" and urged punishment of the mob. In May, reports of an armed clash between the county sheriff's posse and Black residents traced the trouble to the lynching.

ours.title: Lynching of John Risbee and Wyley Lee
ours.accusation: accused of shooting the marshal and a deputy while trying to escape
ours.lead: The lynching of John Risbee and Wyley Lee took place at Chetopa, Kansas, in the early morning of June 27, 1888, when a mob of 200 to 300 men took the two Black men from a sheriff's guard and hanged them from a newspaper office window. The two had been accused of shooting the town marshal and his deputy, both of whom were later reported alive. Papers noted it chiefly for a coroner's jury of four white and eight Black men that split over naming the mob.

ours.title: Lynching of Ben Edwards
ours.accusation: said to have grossly assaulted Miss Catharine Hughes, a white girl, on Friday last
ours.lead: The lynching of Ben Edwards took place at Amite City, Louisiana, on the night of January 28, 1888, when a body of about 100 armed men took Edwards, a Black man, from the town jail and hanged him to a tree. Edwards had been jailed on the accusation that he had criminally assaulted Catherine Hughes, a white girl who lived near the town. A dispatch from Amite City to the New Orleans Times-Democrat ran in papers from California to South Carolina, often under headlines such as "A Fiend Quickly Disposed Of."

ours.title: Lynching of Pony Poe
ours.accusation: accused of criminally assaulting three women of that place
ours.lead: The lynching of Pony Poe was the hanging of a Black man by a mob of about 300 men near Bellefontaine, Webster County, Mississippi, in late August 1888. Poe, accused of assaulting three women, was taken from a sheriff's posse on the way to jail and hanged at the scene of the alleged crime. Newspapers across the country carried the story, many noting that he was a former teacher, a leader of the county's Black residents and a recent candidate for public office.

ours.title: Lynching of Slume and Jonninna
ours.accusation: said to have helped murder three prospectors on Wolf creek last June
ours.lead: The lynching of Slume and Jonninna was the hanging of two Kootenai men by a party of white settlers on the east bank of the Flathead River, opposite Demersville in Missoula County, Montana Territory, in March 1888. The settlers accused the two, with a third Kootenai named Antley who escaped, of killing three prospectors on Wolf Creek the previous summer. The hanging set off a scare of a Kootenai uprising, a petition for federal troops and wire coverage across the country.
