The settlers accused the two, with a third Kootenai named Antley who escaped, of killing three prospectors on Wolf Creek the previous summer. The hanging set off a scare of a Kootenai uprising, a petition for federal troops and wire coverage across the country.

ours.title: Lynching of Sam Cornwall
ours.accusation: said to have quarreled with a white man, Tom Smith; peace warrant issued against him
ours.lead: The lynching of Sam Cornwall was the shooting death of a Black prisoner on a public road in Chester County, South Carolina, in the early morning of September 29 or 30, 1888, while he was in a constable's custody on a peace warrant. His guard said they were fired on from ambush and fled, and a coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of parties unknown. Papers from New York to Texas carried the story, several of them blaming the officers who had left him.

ours.title: Lynching of Archer Cook
ours.accusation: accused of assaulting a white girl
ours.lead: The lynching of Archer Cook was the killing of a Black man, about 22, whom armed and masked men took from the Prince Edward County jail at Farmville, Virginia, early on August 31, 1888, and hanged and shot. Cook had been jailed for months awaiting trial on a charge of assaulting a young white woman, Lizzie Frank. Wire items carried the news across the Midwest and the Dakotas, and a Leavenworth, Kansas, weekly addressed to Black readers urged them to arm and guard the jails.

ours.title: Lynching of Thomas Sayers
ours.accusation: accused of robbery and killing of two white travellers
ours.lead: The lynching of Thomas Sayers took place near Bramwell, Mercer County, West Virginia, around the beginning of November 1888, when a mob took Sayers, a Black man accused of leading a highway robbery, from officers taking him to jail and hanged him from a tree. He had been held for the grand jury after an attack on four white produce sellers in which two were shot. A Post-Dispatch wire carried the news nationally under headlines such as "Negro Murderer Lynched," though reports differed on the date, on whether the robbery victims died, and on how many men were lynched.

found.title: Lynching of a sheepman in Harney Valley, Oregon (1888)
found.accusation: said to have killed a cattle man in a quarrel between cattle and sheep men
found.lead: The lynching of a sheepman in Harney Valley, Oregon, was a killing reported in early January 1888, in which an unnamed sheepman said to have killed a cattleman was himself lynched. A dispatch from The Dalles described the two deaths as a "double homicide" growing out of a quarrel between cattle and sheep men. The only known report is a two-sentence item in the Los Angeles Daily Herald, which gives no names, date or account of the lynchers.

found.title: Lynching of John C. Wells
found.accusation: accused of killing a neighbor in a quarrel about a ditch
found.lead: The lynching of John C. Wells was the reported killing of a Canadian man at Bad Axe, Michigan, by friends of a neighbor whom Wells was said to have killed in a quarrel over a ditch. It was known to the press only through a wire telegram from Kingston, Ontario, in January 1888, which said the matter would be brought to the attention of the Dominion Government.

found.title: Lynching of Julian Medon
found.lead: The lynching of Julian Medon was the hanging of a young Mexican man whose body was found on a tree at Moore's Hill, eleven miles south of Mariposa, California, in late January 1888. The case drew renewed notice in July 1888, when three men were jailed as suspects in what a press dispatch called "plainly a case of lynching."

found.title: Lynching at Gallup, New Mexico (1888)
found.accusation: said to have murdered one or both of his gambling companions
found.lead: The lynching at Gallup, New Mexico, was the killing of an unnamed man by a mob at Gallup in early 1888, after he was accused of murdering one or both of his gambling companions. It is known from a single second-hand item, credited to the Optic and reprinted in the Arizona Silver Belt on February 25, 1888, which drew notice for the mob's use of a passenger coach's bell cord in place of a rope.

found.title: Killing of Jake Marshall, his brother and Louis Payton
found.lead: The killing of Jake Marshall, his brother and Louis Payton took place at Jeanerette, Louisiana, on or shortly before February 7, 1888, when 'unknown persons' shot the three men after Marshall, a Black deputy sheriff, had killed a man named George Dixon. Marshall's brother and Payton, a spectator, died almost at once, and Marshall's body was later found in a swamp ditch. A single special dispatch to the New Orleans Picayune carried the story to papers across the country under headlines counting 'four men' dead.

found.title: Lynching of Aaron Dickey
found.accusation: said to have been involved in debauchery and crime with a white woman
found.lead: The lynching of Aaron Dickey took place at Bluffton, Georgia, shortly before March 4, 1888, when a party of young men tied Dickey, a Black man, to a tree and whipped him until he died. The men acted on the suspicion that Dickey was intimate with a white woman, and a dispatch from Cuthbert that ran in papers from Connecticut to Nevada called the killing "the execution of popular vengeance."

found.title: Cherokee Strip squatter killings
found.lead: The Cherokee Strip squatter killings were the killing of three settlers, named in the first reports as Julius Quinn, William Antwerp and Joseph George, by cowboys of the cattleman George H. Delaney in the Cherokee Strip of the Indian Territory in early March 1888. Wichita dispatches said the men were burned out of their cabin and shot; a deputy U.S. marshal's account added a woman and a cowboy to the dead. The story ran nationally, and later dispatches reported two cattlemen lynched in reprisal.

found.title: Lynching of John Wood
found.accusation: accused of abducting Amelia Wilson, a white girl
found.lead: The lynching of John Wood was the reported killing of a Black man at Denison, Texas, on March 28, 1888. Wood was accused of abducting Amelia Wilson, described as a white girl, and was said to have been lynched for it. The case reached readers only as a one-sentence wire item and as a line in a year-end roll of lynching victims.

found.title: Lynching of Joseph Prescott
found.accusation: said to have attempted to break into a store at Dillon's Bridge
found.lead: The lynching of Joseph Prescott was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a band of white "regulators" in southeastern Pike County, Mississippi, near Dillon's Bridge, after midnight on the night of Sunday, April 8, 1888. The same band reportedly beat Frank Warner, a Black boy of about fifteen, into accusing Prescott and the brothers Hardy and Ben Kaigler of trying to rob a store, then whipped the Kaiglers. A coroner's jury charged twenty-four white men and seventeen were arrested, while residents near the scene publicly disputed the Magnolia Gazette's account.

found.title: Healdton lynchings (1888)
found.accusation: said to have been connected with a gang of horsethieves
found.lead: The Healdton lynchings were the hanging of Bill Morgan and two or three other men by a mob of citizens near Healdton, in the Chickasaw Nation of Indian Territory, on the night of Monday, April 9, 1888. The men were accused of belonging to a band of horse thieves, and federal deputy marshals afterward arrested some of those said to have been in the mob. Newspapers in Texas and across the country carried the news from Gainesville, Texas, and the case was later entered in year-end tallies of lynchings.

found.title: Lynching of Bill Parkman
found.accusation: accused of said to have burglarized the house of Mr. Bryan
found.lead: The lynching of Bill Parkman was the killing of a Black prisoner accused of burglary, taken with Henry Williams from his guards at Raleigh, Meriwether County, Georgia, in April 1888 by fifteen or twenty armed men. Parkman's beaten and burned body was found the next morning near Cane Creek. Williams, at first reported lynched too, turned up alive days later.

found.title: Lynching of Henry Pope
found.accusation: accused of said to have raped Miss Kendrick (Hendricks)
found.lead: The lynching of Henry Pope took place at Summerville, Chattooga county, Georgia, on the night of April 30-May 1, 1888, when a mob of about fifty masked men took Pope, a Black prisoner, from the county jail and hanged him from the court-house banisters. Pope had twice been convicted of assaulting a young white woman, Minnie Kendrick, and had been respited by Governor Gordon days before his scheduled execution on evidence that he had been in Alabama at the time. The killing was reported across the country, and one Atlanta dispatch called Pope an innocent man.

found.title: Lynching of James Hicks
found.accusation: accused of attempted outrage on a little 7-year-old girl
found.lead: The lynching of James Hicks was the killing of a Black man by Black neighbors near Port Gibson, Mississippi, reported in early May 1888. Accused of attempting to outrage a 7-year-old girl, Hicks was whipped by the girl's father and then shot and hanged by neighbors who judged the whipping insufficient. The story ran as a brief in distant papers, one headed "Summary Punishment."

found.title: Lynching of Manuel Bowers
found.accusation: accused of said to have shot and killed Chas. Huguely near Indian Village
found.lead: The lynching of Manuel Bowers was the hanging of a Black man to a tree in his own yard in Louisiana in May 1888, a few days after a posse captured him near Coushatta. Bowers was accused of shooting and killing Chas. Huguely near Indian Village about two weeks earlier. The only account found is a single sentence in a weekly paper's column of state news, which named no one in the hanging party.

found.title: Lynching in Claiborne County, Mississippi (1888)
found.accusation: said to have committed rape
found.lead: The lynching in Claiborne County, Mississippi, was the punishment of an unnamed Black man accused of rape by "Judge Lynch" in the week before May 5, 1888. It is known from a single sentence in the Grenada Sentinel, which paired it with a lynching at Vicksburg and did not say what was done to the man.

found.title: Rhea County quadruple lynching
found.accusation: accused of said to have assaulted a white woman and her daughter
found.lead: The Rhea County quadruple lynching was the reported killing by a mob, in May 1888, of four Black men held in the jail at Washington, the seat of Rhea County, Tennessee, after they were accused of assaulting a white woman and her daughter. A Chattanooga dispatch named the four as James Strickland, Nick Webster, Jerry Long and Sam Sibner and predicted that a mob would lynch them; a day later, a Spring City special reported that it had. Every report of the lynching was second-hand, and the coverage contains no local confirmation, inquest or arrests.

found.title: Killing of Arthur Harton
found.lead: The killing of Arthur Harton took place near Curtis, Arkansas, in May 1888, when five Black men took Harton, a Black man, from his bed and beat him to death with an iron bar in a nearby thicket. Four of the five were arrested, and the papers that carried the story drew attention to the fact that three of the men were preachers. A later news summary said Harton had been accused of immorality.

found.title: Killing of Joshua Anderson
found.lead: The killing of Joshua Anderson was the fatal stabbing of a farmer near Owensboro, Kentucky, in late spring 1888 by one of four men who had disguised themselves as "White Caps" to whip him. The men were said to have whipped Anderson once and ordered him to leave, then killed him when they tried to whip him a second time; the principals were arrested.

found.title: Lynching of an unnamed Black man at Grand Forks, Dakota
found.accusation: accused of raping a white woman
found.lead: The lynching of an unnamed Black man at Grand Forks, Dakota, was a mob killing reported only in a June 1888 editorial in the Western Appeal of St. Paul, Minnesota, which dated it to "only a short time ago." According to the editorial, the man was accused of raping a white woman, pursued into Minnesota by a mob, taken back to Grand Forks and torn apart by teams of horses. The paper cited the case as proof that lynching for alleged rape reached "even up here, in the free Northwest," and said the woman later admitted he had not raped her.

found.title: Lynching of Frank Lang'y
found.accusation: said to have murdered half a dozen people and stolen hundreds of head of cattle
found.lead: The lynching of Frank Lang'y was the hanging, in Oklahoma in about May or June 1888, of a man described as an outlaw, after local people took him from the officers who held him. It is known from a single brief in the Turner County Herald of Hurley, Dakota, which gave no date beyond 'recently' and no place more exact than Oklahoma.

found.title: Lynching of Morgan Williams
found.accusation: said to have killed Morgan Jones in self-defense against his attacks
found.lead: The lynching of Morgan Williams was the killing of a Black man by a group of Black men in Canton, Mississippi, in late July 1888. According to the only report found, Williams, a stranger in the town, had killed a man named Morgan Jones while defending himself against Jones's attacks. The report named the lynchers only as "negroes" and treated the episode as one item among the week's state news.

found.title: Lynching of James Hagley
found.accusation: said to have attempted to assault Belle Simms, aged 11 years
found.lead: The lynching of James Hagley was the shooting death of a Black man at Alma, Arkansas, on the night of July 2-3, 1888, after he was taken from the town jail at midnight. He had been held on an accusation of attempting to assault a 12-year-old girl, and according to a wire dispatch he was tied to a tree and "slowly shot to pieces." The killing reached distant newspapers only as a one-sentence telegraphic item.

found.title: Lynching of John Humphreys
found.lead: The lynching of John Humphreys took place at Asheville, North Carolina, in the early morning of 15 July 1888, when a band of twenty-five to forty masked men broke into the county jail, took out the Black prisoner and hanged him to a tree. Humphreys had been arrested the night before, accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old white girl, and was hanged before any trial. The Charlotte Democrat called it the first lynching known in Western North Carolina, and the Asheville dispatch was reprinted across the country.

found.title: Killing of Lewis C. Lane
found.lead: The killing of Lewis C. Lane took place near Quitman, Georgia, on July 16, 1888, when W. T. Arrington overtook a sheriff who was moving Lane, a Savannah traveling salesman charged with assaulting Arrington's daughter, to the Thomasville jail and shot him dead. Arrington and his brother-in-law Henry T. Williams were later charged with murder and released on bail, and no report of a trial was found. The Savannah Morning News covered the case at length because Lane was well known there, and a letter in its columns called the killing lynch law.

found.title: Lynching of Dr. G. H. Thomas
found.accusation: said to have outraged Miss Amelia Shives
found.lead: The lynching of Dr. G. H. Thomas was the killing by a mob of a man who called himself Dr. G. H. Thomas, near Oxford, Mississippi, in the early hours of July 17, 1888, after he had been arrested and placed under guard at the farm where he boarded. He was accused of drugging and "ruining" Amelia Shives, his host's daughter, whom he had treated as a physician. Wire reports told the story as the lynching of "a Rapist," but a meeting of citizens east of Oxford condemned the killing as done "without cause or provocation" and called for an investigation.

found.title: Shooting of John Grayson
found.accusation: accused of shooting Lilburn Trigg
found.lead: The shooting of John Grayson took place in Abingdon, Virginia, on the evening of Saturday, July 21, 1888, when Grayson, who had just shot a local man named Lilburn Trigg, was hit by a pistol ball fired by an unidentified person as a crowd chased him. Grayson died the next morning, Trigg three days later, and Trigg's mother of shock that night, and newspapers called it a triple tragedy. The Richmond Dispatch's Abingdon correspondent wrote that Grayson would have been lynched had he survived.

found.title: Lynching of Bruce Younger
found.accusation: accused of ravishing a white married woman
found.lead: The lynching of Bruce Younger was the killing of a Black man by a party of armed horsemen who took him from the jail at Halifax Court House, Virginia, around midnight on July 26–27, 1888, and hanged and shot him at a nearby footbridge. Younger had been arrested the day before, accused of assaulting Mrs. Robert Dodd, the wife of the farmer near Meadsville for whom he worked. The story went out on the wire under a Danville dateline, and some news digests placed the lynching at Danville itself.

found.title: Burning of a Mojave woman accused of witchcraft (1888)
found.accusation: said to have practiced witchcraft
found.lead: The burning of a Mojave woman accused of witchcraft was the reported killing, in late summer 1888, of an unnamed Mojave woman of about eighteen by members of her tribe in eastern San Bernardino County, California. According to the reports, the band's leaders judged her a witch, and she was tied to a stake and burned, dying after about two hours. The story reached the press through two Los Angeles accounts in mid-September and ran nationally under headlines about Indian "barbarism" and revived witch burning.

found.title: Killing of Martin Wilson
found.accusation: accused of attempting to outrage a white woman
found.lead: The killing of Martin Wilson was the shooting of a Black man by a posse at a place printed as Malton, Alabama, reported at the end of August 1888. He was accused of having attempted to assault a white woman, and the only known report gave that accusation as the reason he was killed.

found.title: Lynching of Will Robinson
found.accusation: said to have made an assault with intent to outrage a white woman
found.lead: The lynching of Will Robinson was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of about 100 people at Staton's stretch, Tallahatchie County, Mississippi, on the morning of August 8, 1888. Robinson had been accused of attempting to assault a white woman, and the only report found, a Dublin dispatch printed in the Grenada Sentinel, said he confessed before he was hanged "without law or ceremony."

found.title: Lynching near Big Cypress Bayou, Bossier Parish (1888)
found.accusation: accused of breaking into a store and stealing a sum of money
found.lead: The lynching near Big Cypress Bayou was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a mob near Big Cypress Bayou in Bossier Parish, Louisiana, on Tuesday, August 14, 1888. He was accused of breaking into a store and stealing a sum of money. The report reached the national press mainly as a short addendum to dispatches about the killing of Black people by 'regulators' near Freetown.

found.title: Braswell trestle lynching
found.accusation: accused of gross immorality with a negro woman
found.lead: The Braswell trestle lynching was the hanging of an unnamed Black man from a railroad trestle at Braswell, Georgia, printed as "Beaswell" in wire reports, on the night of August 25, 1888. He had been accused of "gross immorality" with a Black woman, and an informant told a correspondent that the lynchers were a mixed crowd of white and Black men. Wire dispatches carried the killing to papers as far away as Dakota as a "mysterious lynching."

found.title: Lynching of William Martin
found.accusation: accused of said to have committed a brutal assault on Mrs. McClellan, and of meaning to kill the entire McClellan family
found.lead: The lynching of William Martin was the killing of a Black man near Rome, Covington County, Alabama, in late summer 1888, after he was taken from a deputy sheriff who was moving him to Florida. Martin, accused of assaulting a white woman, was shot and his body thrown into an old well, and the story ran as a brief wire item in Georgia and Kansas papers.

found.title: Deer Creek vigilante killing of horse thieves
found.accusation: horse-stealing
found.lead: The Deer Creek vigilante killing of horse thieves was the reported destruction, around August 31 or September 1, 1888, of a camp of sixteen to eighteen men accused of horse and cattle theft by forty to fifty armed vigilantes in the Public Land Strip, or 'No Man's Land'. Three vigilantes were also reported killed. Carried by wire from Kansas City, the story ran in dozens of papers as a battle in which 'no quarter was asked or given', though no paper in the region could supply particulars.

found.title: Killing of Gus Saddler
found.accusation: said to have committed an outrage on a little white girl
found.lead: The killing of Gus Saddler was the shooting of a young Black man by an unknown person at Bagdad, Calcasieu Parish, Louisiana, on September 2, 1888, while he was held by a crowd of local citizens. The crowd had seized him after he was accused of raping a six-year-old white girl and forced a confession from him by staging a mock hanging. A coroner's jury found that he had been killed by an unknown party, and the Lake Charles Commercial presented the death as "Swift Retribution."

found.title: Lynching of Frank Gillam and George Elliott
found.accusation: said to have been involved in stealing horses
found.lead: The lynching of Frank Gillam and George Elliott was the reported hanging of two men accused of horse theft by cowmen in Routt county, Colorado, near the Utah line, in mid-September 1888. The news reached Aspen, where Gillam had lived, as rumor, but papers in Colorado and Montana repeated it as fact.

found.title: Lynching of Frank Easterling
found.accusation: said to have stolen cotton (Frank); accused of harboring Frank (Sharp)
found.lead: The lynching of Frank Easterling took place on the night of Saturday, October 6, 1888, in Rankin County, Mississippi, when a mob took Easterling, a Black man, out and hanged him and shot Sharper Easterling, at whose house he was found. Mississippi papers gave two motives: the first reports said Frank was killed for saying he would vote Democratic, while later briefs said he was accused of stealing cotton.

found.title: Lynching at Marion, Louisiana (1888)
found.accusation: said to have been implicated in the killing of Luther Hayes
found.lead: The lynching at Marion, Louisiana, was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a party of men pursuing a suspect in the killing of Luther Hayes, a white man, around October 29, 1888. The man was said to have been implicated in the killing in some way, while the accused shooter, Nathan Broadnax, remained at large. The only known report, carried by the Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe, also passed on expectations that more Black men near Marion would be killed.

found.title: Lynching of Henry Cook
found.accusation: said to have broken into the home of a widow named Jones while intoxicated and outraged her twelve-year-old daughter
found.lead: The lynching of Henry Cook took place on the night of Sunday, November 11, 1888, in the swamps of Miller County, Georgia, where a group of men ran him down and killed him. Cook had been accused of breaking into a widow's home while drunk and assaulting her 12-year-old daughter. The killing was known only through a short dispatch from Bainbridge, Georgia, which ran in a few papers in Tennessee, Kentucky and Florida.

found.title: Lynching of Bob Bonner
found.accusation: said to have outraged a twelve-year-old colored girl
found.lead: The lynching of Bob Bonner took place at Petersburg, Tennessee, on the night of Friday, November 16, 1888, when five armed masked men took Bonner, a Black prisoner, from the town jail and hanged him half a mile from town. He had been arrested the night before on a charge of outraging a twelve-year-old Black girl. A Nashville wire brief carried the news to papers from Virginia to Minnesota and New Hampshire, while a Tennessee weekly called it "a first class lynching."

found.title: Killing of William Durant and lynching of Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis
found.lead: The killing of William Durant and lynching of Silas Jeffries and Abe Davis took place near Tushomma, Indian Territory, in November 1888, when a stockman was shot dead outside his home and his friends then hunted down and killed two neighbors suspected of leading his killers. Three men died, and no arrest, inquest or trial appears in the coverage. A single wire dispatch from Little Rock, Arkansas, carried the story to papers from Washington to St. Paul, where headlines called the second killings a "lynching", "retaliation" or the work of "avengers".

found.title: Westport hanging of two men (1888)
found.accusation: said to have been horse thieves
found.lead: The Westport hanging of two men was the discovery, reported on the evening of December 12, 1888, of the bodies of two unidentified men hanging from a tree near a school house south of Westport, in Jackson County, Missouri. Newspapers supposed the men were horse thieves lynched by farmers, vigilantes or an anti-horse-thief association, but no report named the dead or the men who hanged them. The item ran as a brief in papers from Minnesota and Kansas to California, Wisconsin, Dakota and Rhode Island over the following ten days.

found.title: Lynching of W. D. French
found.accusation: accused of murdering Harry Woodbury
found.lead: The lynching of W. D. French took place in Greeley, Colorado, on the night of December 28-29, 1888, when a body of masked men broke into the county jail, took out French and hanged him to a tree. French, a cattle owner and farmer, was being held with three other men for the killing of Harry Woodbury at Evans about two weeks earlier. No member of the mob was identified, and most papers reported the lynching only as a short wire item.

broad_only.title: Warren settlement-dispute killings
broad_only.lead: The Warren settlement-dispute killings were the reported killing of one Black man and the mortal wounding of another in Arkansas shortly before mid-January 1888, after a "squad" went to a Black man's house following a debt dispute with a white man named Gorman. The only account, a short item in an Arkansas news column, rested on rumor and named none of the dead, the wounded or the attackers.

broad_only.title: Burning of Randall McCoy's house
broad_only.lead: The burning of Randall McCoy's house was a night attack on McCoy's home on the Blackberry Fork of Pond Creek, Pike County, Kentucky, on or about January 1, 1888, in which attackers fired the house and shot the family as they came out. McCoy's daughter and a son were killed and his wife badly wounded; McCoy escaped. Papers across the country blamed the Hatfields of Logan County, West Virginia, as the latest act of the Hatfield-McCoy feud, though a Logan County state senator denied they took part.

broad_only.title: Killing of George Madden and the Winona lynching mob
victims: two unnamed friends of Rucker (reported lynched)
broad_only.accusation: said to have shot and killed Constable John Rucker
broad_only.lead: The killing of George Madden and the Winona lynching mob was an episode of mob violence at Winona, Shannon County, Missouri, in early March 1888, in which railroad laborers hunted Constable John Rucker after he was reported to have shot and killed the subcontractor George Madden. No report of Rucker's fate appears in the coverage, and a single Springfield dispatch said the laborers caught and lynched two of his friends and shot a third. Most papers carried the story as a St. Louis wire report of an "atrocious murder" followed by a "howling mob."

broad_only.title: Killing of Archie Stokes at the Woodlawn road convict camp
broad_only.lead: The killing of Archie Stokes at the Woodlawn road convict camp took place on the morning of March 24, 1888, near Birmingham, Alabama, when deputy sheriffs fired on a squad of leased county convicts who had refused to work. Stokes, a Black convict, was killed and a second convict, Henry Allen, was wounded, and a coroner's jury found the shooting was done in performance of duty. Papers around the country carried the story as the suppression of a convict "mutiny".

broad_only.title: Killing of Hunley Royl
broad_only.lead: The killing of Hunley Royl was the assassination of an elderly Black man living near Newport, Arkansas, by a party of masked men, reported in early March 1888. The only account found is a single line in a weekly state news column, which gave no date, motive or follow-up.

broad_only.title: Killing of Jim Harrington
broad_only.lead: The killing of Jim Harrington was the shooting of a Black farm worker by four masked men near Farmerville, Louisiana, on the evening of Friday, March 30, 1888. The men took him from the field where he was plowing, led him into the Loutre swamp with a rope around his neck, and shot him; a coroner's investigation could not identify them. The local paper called it "a murder surrounded with mystery."

broad_only.title: Killing of two Black men near Spanish Camp, Texas (March 1888)
broad_only.lead: The killing of two Black men near Spanish Camp, Texas, took place on a plantation in Wharton County in the third week of March 1888, a few weeks after a massacre of Black residents at the same settlement. The victims were not named and no one was reported arrested. Papers treated the killings as fresh proof of a 'reign of terror' against the county's Black population that state rangers had failed to stop.

broad_only.title: Shooting into the Essex Dargan house
victims: unnamed three-year-old child of Essex Dargan
broad_only.accusation: said to have shot and killed a white boy (Dock Dorgar, Black boy)
broad_only.lead: The shooting into the Essex Dargan house took place near Bennettsville, in Marlboro County, South Carolina, at the end of April 1888, when a number of men fired into the home of a Black man whose son was jailed for killing a white youth and killed a three-year-old child. The son, Dock Dargan, was not harmed by the men; a wire dispatch said several attempts had been made to lynch him, while the local paper spoke only of rumors. He was hanged at Bennettsville that September.

broad_only.title: Killing of W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove
broad_only.lead: The killing of W. E. Ashley and Eugene Grove was the hanging of Grove and shooting of Ashley, two men from Belvidere, Kansas, by a band of vigilantes a few miles below Englewood in the Indian Territory, reported in late April 1888. Grove was hanged at the vigilantes' camp and Ashley was shot dead after he opened fire, while two women travelling with them were never accounted for. A single Belvidere dispatch carried the story from Washington to the Kansas weeklies, and its closing judgment that vigilantes were "worse than those whom they seek to kill" made it a small case against frontier vigilantism.

broad_only.title: Killing of Charles Gross
broad_only.accusation: said to have divulged secrets of the Agricultural Wheel, a secret organization
broad_only.lead: The killing of Charles Gross was the whipping to death of a farmer in Pulaski County, Missouri, by a band of masked night riders on the night of June 23, 1888. The cause assigned in the dispatches was that Gross had revealed the secrets of the Agricultural Wheel, a secret organization. Papers across the country ran the story as an outrage by a band likened to the White Caps of Indiana, and one dispatch reported arrests, but no later account of a prosecution was found.

broad_only.title: Lynching of John Lynn
broad_only.lead: The lynching of John Lynn was the killing of a Black man by a mob of thirty-five armed white men at his home in Assumption Parish, Louisiana, in late July 1888. Lynn shot dead one of the attackers before he was captured, and the mob later shot him in twelve places. A New Orleans telegram presented it as one of a series of 'outrages against the blacks' that had prompted talk of an exodus.

broad_only.title: Freetown killings (1888)
broad_only.accusation: said to have stirred up trouble among the negroes
broad_only.lead: The Freetown killings took place on August 16, 1888, when an armed body of white men from three south Louisiana parishes besieged a house in Freetown, a Black settlement in Iberia Parish, and shot dead between ten and twenty Black men who had armed themselves there. One white attacker, the New Iberia civil engineer E. Payson Smith, was killed while forcing the door. The affair became a partisan issue: Southern papers called it a 'war of races', while Northern Republican papers and a senator called it murder.

broad_only.title: Lynching of Harrison Spencer
broad_only.lead: The lynching of Harrison Spencer was the abduction and killing of a Black farmer and local politician near Longview, Gregg County, Texas, in late August 1888 by a masked band that took him from his home at night. His body was found several days later hanging from a tree on Harris Creek, shot, whipped and mutilated. Papers tied the killing to his break with the Union Labor party, and the case was read into a United States Senate debate as an example of political murder in Texas.

broad_only.title: 1888 election violence in Union County, Arkansas
broad_only.lead: The 1888 election violence in Union County, Arkansas, was a series of floggings, beatings and reported killings of Black men by armed Democrats around the state election of September 3, 1888, centered on El Dorado. Press Neal, Sandy Newton and Aaron Cobb were among the men named as whipped, while the dead went unnamed and estimates ran from one or two Black men to a rumored sixteen. Northern Republican papers held up the county as an example of how the Democrats had carried Arkansas.

broad_only.title: Round Mountain ambush (1888)
broad_only.lead: The Round Mountain ambush was a shooting at Round Mountain, Cherokee County, Alabama, in September 1888, in which a white man, George Whitt, and his friends were reported to have fired from ambush on five Black men, killing two and wounding three. An armed battle between the two sides followed later that night, with several people reported killed and wounded on both sides. Newspapers from New York to California ran the report as a "race war."

broad_only.title: Killing of Ernest Williams
broad_only.accusation: said to have been in a row in a Fourth street dive and to be fleeing arrest
broad_only.lead: The killing of Ernest Williams was the fatal shooting of a Black man in Macon, Georgia, on September 4, 1888, as an excited crowd chased him after he ran from an attempted arrest. Accounts of who fired differed, and at the coroner's inquest the next day three Black witnesses named a white man, Daniel Lucas, as the shooter.

broad_only.title: Lynching of William Lewis
broad_only.lead: The lynching of William Lewis was the hanging of a Black man by unknown persons near Durant, Mississippi, whose body was found on a tree on the morning of September 4, 1888. No cause was assigned and the perpetrators were not identified. The case reached readers only as a brief wire item, printed in Savannah and in several Northern papers the next day.

broad_only.title: Killing of T. C. Yates
broad_only.lead: The killing of T. C. Yates was the shooting of a man described as "a noted desperado" in the Chickasaw Nation, Indian Territory, on or about September 1, 1888. According to a wire dispatch from Little Rock, Arkansas, Yates fired into a crowd, people in the crowd fired back, and he fell dead from his horse. Papers across the country printed the item as a short brief, and one Kentucky paper condensed it to a line saying he had been "killed by a mob."

broad_only.title: Breaux Bridge night raid
broad_only.lead: The Breaux Bridge night raid was an attack on the night of September 14, 1888, in which four or five armed men went to Black cabins near Breaux Bridge, Louisiana, killed a Black woman, whipped a Black man, and sexually assaulted a Black woman. Five men were arrested; one, Sam Polk, turned state's witness and named Vilmont Hollier as the man who fired, and two were held without bail. The killing was carried by wire across the country and was cited in the United States Senate as political violence.

broad_only.title: Killing of Caesar Stevens
broad_only.lead: The killing of Caesar Stevens was the shooting of a Black laborer by a group of armed white men in a garden at Branchville, South Carolina, on October 8, 1888. Stevens was struck nine times and died the next morning, and the three men named as the shooters were not arrested in the days that followed. Papers in South Carolina and Georgia called it a cold-blooded murder and singled out the lack of arrests.

broad_only.title: Lynching of Wilson Arnold
broad_only.accusation: accused of the murder of Captain Robert Johnson
broad_only.lead: The lynching of Wilson Arnold was the killing of a Black man, also named in the papers as Wilkes or Wilks Arnold, who was taken from the jail at Yazoo City, Mississippi, by an armed mob on November 19, 1888, and hanged. Arnold had surrendered to the sheriff about a week earlier after shooting Captain Robert Johnson, a white planter, near Satartia, a killing he said was in self-defense. A Yazoo County grand jury later reported that it could not identify any of the lynchers, although about fifteen were said to be known.

broad_only.title: Pittsville church shooting
broad_only.lead: The Pittsville church shooting was an attack in October 1888 in which a crowd of armed young white men rode up to a Black church at Pittsville, in Fort Bend County, Texas, called the congregation out and fired into it. Lamar Johnson was killed and Taylor Randon was wounded. The Galveston News called it a political assassination and blamed the Jay Bird Club, a new Democratic organization, while a leading Fort Bend Democrat denied that politics played any part.

broad_only.title: Attempted lynching of John Glenn
broad_only.accusation: accused of said to have assaulted a little girl near a school
broad_only.lead: The attempted lynching of John Glenn took place at Sandy Hill, Washington County, New York, on November 7, 1888, when a crowd tried to seize Glenn, a baseball player accused of assaulting a nine-year-old girl, from the policemen who had arrested him. In the struggle a policeman's revolver went off and the ball struck Glenn in the neck; most reports called the shooting accidental, while one wire brief said a member of the mob fired. A Vermont paper reported a week later that Glenn had died.

broad_only.title: Killing of Jeff Davis's wife at Lake City
broad_only.lead: The killing of Jeff Davis's wife at Lake City was the fatal stabbing of a Black woman by three white men near Lake City, Williamsburg County, South Carolina, reported in November 1888. She was killed while trying to protect her son, whom the men were beating, and the dispatch reporting the killing said the attackers remained at large with no effort made to arrest them.

broad_only.title: Tackett's Mills riot
broad_only.lead: The Tackett's Mills riot was a fight between white and Black men at a country store at Tackett's Mills, Stafford County, Virginia, on Christmas Day 1888. A white man, Bennett (or Benton) Heflin, was shot dead, and a Black man, named Henry Brown in a later report, died of his injuries. Papers across the country reported it as a 'race riot' arising from the recent election, and Fredericksburg feared further trouble.

broad_only.title: Killing of Adam Golden
broad_only.lead: The killing of Adam Golden occurred on a Monday night in December 1888, when a masked mob stoning the house of Jennie Maddox, seven miles north of Buchanan in Haralson County, Georgia, beat and shot to death Golden, a Black man who had intervened. Five white men and two Black men were jailed for the murder and three white women were held for taking part. The story ran on the telegraph across the country, where it appeared beside reports of White Cap outrages and under headlines such as "Killed for His Interference."

broad_only.title: Sim McCoy raid
broad_only.lead: The Sim McCoy raid was a reported attack by the "Hatfield gang" on the home of Sim McCoy, a brother of Randall McCoy, in Wyoming County, West Virginia, on a Saturday night in mid-January 1888. According to dispatches from Charleston and Parkersburg, the raiders tied Mrs. McCoy to a tree and shot her, killed a son, and burned McCoy, and by some accounts two young children, in the house. Papers across the country printed it as a new chapter of the Hatfield-McCoy feud, but every account was relayed from word reaching other towns, and the deaths of the children were never confirmed.

broad_only.title: Killing of Mack Henry
broad_only.lead: The killing of Mack Henry was the fatal shooting of a Black man by an unknown assailant near Ichetuchnee, Florida, on Friday, July 27, 1888. The only known report, from the Lake City correspondent of the Savannah Morning News, noted that Henry's wife had been shot and killed at the same place about three months earlier.

broad_only.title: Killing of Levi Lally
broad_only.lead: The killing of Levi Lally was the fatal shooting of a farmer at his house near Montevallo, Alabama, on the night of Saturday, July 21, 1888, by two white men and a Black man who had called him outside. Lally died the next day, and warrants were issued on suspicion against men with whom he had quarrelled over work. The case reached distant papers through a single Montgomery dispatch, and a moonshiner killing in Bibb County, reported about ten days later, bore some resemblance to it.

broad_only.title: Killing of Margaret Auxier
broad_only.lead: The killing of Margaret Auxier was the shooting death of a young woman by a party of men at her father's house near Yocum, Morgan County, Kentucky, in early March 1888. Several men were held on suspicion and lynching was talked of, and in August a man charged with the crime was himself found murdered after saying he would turn State's evidence.

broad_only.title: Death of an unidentified man in the Boston Mountains, Arkansas (1888)
broad_only.lead: In February 1888 two hunters found the body of an unidentified, heavily armed man in the Boston Mountains of Arkansas, near a still where a revenue collector had killed its owner the previous fall. No marks showed how he died, but newspapers supposed he was a detective gathering evidence against illicit distilling and headlined the death "Murdered by Moonshiners."
